title: Low-cost soil moisture sensors for smallholder irrigation scheduling: a field comparison

headings.text: Low-cost soil moisture sensors for smallholder irrigation scheduling: a field comparison

key_sentences: Smallholder farmers rarely measure soil moisture because commercial probes are expensive.
Irrigation scheduled from the cheaper sensors used 23 percent less water than the farmers' usual practice with no loss of yield.
Over-watering wastes pumping energy and leaches nitrogen, while under-watering during flowering reduces yield sharply.
This paper reports a season-long comparison carried out on working farms rather than on an experimental station.
Soils ranged from a sandy loam to a clay loam, and each farm irrigated from its own shallow well.
A data logger recorded the raw readings every thirty minutes and sent a daily summary by text message.
Both capacitive sensors reached a root mean square error close to two volumetric percentage points.
The main cost of a useful low-cost system is not the sensor but the calibration visit.
Farmers valued the daily text message more than the raw numbers, and three of them asked to keep the loggers after the trial.
Further work will test the sensors in maize and over two consecutive seasons.
